observations.quote: it is repugnant neither to Nature nor Reason that a Man may prolong his life beyond the common ordinary age of Men, even to a long time
observations.note: Croll holds that life may be lengthened beyond the ordinary age, as agreeing with Nature and Reason; he grants it may pass for the discourse of Vaine men.

observations.quote: and that for two Reasons
observations.note: Announces a numbered pair of reasons; the first opens CH6.70, the second CH6.71.

observations.quote: Tis possible to extend a long life farther
observations.note: The margin restates the claim of CH6.69.

observations.name: Porta
observations.quote: Porta reject the opinion of those that cast mens fortune from the day or houre of their nativity prefixing the bounds of life
observations.note: The note gives Porta as rejecting those who fix the bounds of life from the day or hour of birth, and as affirming that one wary of his infirmities may live longer.

observations.name: Parac.
observations.quote: Parac. chap. 7. of the Labyrinth of Physitians
observations.note: The note closes by naming a chapter of a writing of Parac. beside the claim that life may be prolonged.

observations.quote: in NATURALS there is no certaine appointed Terme apparent what day we shall die, but it is in our own hand and power to put an end to our life if we will, and to prolong it
observations.note: First reason: in natural things no appointed day of death is apparent; ending or prolonging life lies in our own power, and prolonging it is said to be without offence to GOD.

observations.quote: I speak here Phylosophically of the Naturall death
observations.note: Croll says in which sense his words are meant: Phylosophically, of the Naturall death, not Theologically of the Fatall death.

observations.quote: the Naturall death, which is onely the wasting of the Naturall Moysture and Heat, as may be seen in a burning lamp
observations.note: The text says what Naturall death is: the wasting of the Naturall Moysture and Heat, likened to a burning lamp.

observations.quote: the Fatall death and utmost Terme which God hath prefixt to every one, by which we are inforc'd not onely to pay the debt of Nature, but are compel'd also to undergoe the punishment for sin
observations.note: The Fatall death is the utmost Terme God has prefixed to every one, by which the debt of Nature is paid and the punishment for sin undergone; it is set apart from the Naturall death.

observations.quote: Death is the Bound which we cannot passe, nor is there any day or hour, for by the Grace of God we live the Terme without houres
observations.note: Death is a bound that cannot be passed, yet no day or hour of it is set.

observations.quote: As God hath numbred our hairs, so also doth he reckon our years, leaving them in our power
observations.note: God reckons our years and leaves them in our power.

observations.quote: a long and lasting life of Man in this world is not displeasing to him, especially if it be spent in the Fear and Service of his Creator
observations.note: A long life does not displease God, the more so if spent in his fear and service; the text draws this from God's pleasure that Man should live for ever and from the propagation of Mankind.

observations.quote: that utmost and fixed Terme or determined poynt of DIVINE PREDESTINATION which is unknown to mortalls
observations.note: The fixed Terme of DIVINE PREDESTINATION is unknown to mortals; a long life always stays short of it. Kind corrected from concealment: the text speaks of a limit unknown to men, not of knowledge withheld.

observations.quote: imposed on our first Parents and their heires, for their Fall from Originall Righteousnesse, beyond which Bound no man can goe.
observations.note: The fixed Terme was imposed on the first Parents and their heirs for their Fall; no man can go beyond it.

observations.quote: so may he prolong his life by removing these impediments, so that at last he may attaine to the appointed Terme of the Nature of life
observations.note: As diseases may shorten a man's time, so removing these impediments lets him reach the appointed Terme of the Nature of life.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: See Paracelsus of long life
observations.note: The margin points to a writing of Paracelsus beside the passage on the fixed Terme unknown to mortals.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: See Paracelsus in lib. 8
observations.note: The margin points to Paracelsus, lib. 8, beside the Bound no man can pass; the note does not say of which writing.

observations.name: Archid.
observations.quote: Archid. of the Elixirs
observations.note: The note opens by naming a writing, Archid. of the Elixirs, beside the words on life compassed about with diseases; the lines after it may be drawn from it, the note does not show.

observations.quote: It is the conservation of the Human body from all accidentall corruption
observations.note: The note says of something that it is the conservation of the human body from all accidental corruption; it follows the words of the Elixirs, but the note does not name what It is.

observations.quote: There is a two fold death, from the Iliad or first principle, and from the Ens or Being
observations.note: Two deaths are set apart by their source: the Iliad and the Ens.

observations.quote: from the Iliad or first principle
observations.note: Iliad is glossed as first principle.

observations.quote: from the Ens or Being
observations.note: Ens is glossed as Being.

observations.quote: The Soule of perpetuity or the Spirit of Light joyned to Nature with the light is perpetuall, and will not suffer such a conjunction and such a life to be short
observations.note: The Soule of perpetuity, also called the Spirit of Light, joined to Nature is perpetual and does not let such a life be short.

observations.quote: God hath created the aforesaid Medicine for the preservation of life
observations.note: Second reason. The Medicine is called aforesaid: the text points back to an earlier place; the lines given do not show which.

observations.quote: which may preserve our body as well from the corruption of our Parents, as from the defect of our own government, cure its infirmities, and repaire what is wasted
observations.note: What the Medicine does: keeps the body from inherited corruption and from faults of our own government, cures infirmities, repairs what is wasted, and chases away the diseases that cause the naturall death.

observations.quote: ultimate death the most Terrible of all Terrible things (which is the destruction of the Mummy) which God the most high Creator hath ordained as the wages of sinners
observations.note: Ultimate death is the destruction of the Mummy, ordained by God as the wages of sinners; the Medicine works until this death.

observations.name: Paracelsus
observations.quote: Paracelsus saith that the death which is from the resolution of the Iliad may be hindred by the industry of the Physitian, but that which is from the Ens or Being cannot
observations.note: Paracelsus is given as saying that death from the resolution of the Iliad can be hindered by the physician, death from the Ens or Being cannot.

observations.quote: as we may preserve a little fire by laying on more wood; so also may our life be prolonged by administring such Remedies and secrets as are derived from the fountaine of Gods gifts
observations.note: Life is prolonged by Remedies and secrets as a small fire is kept by laying on wood. The words follow 'Paracelsus saith' after a colon; the text does not show whether they are still his. Kind corrected from local signal: a comparison, not a signal how to read.

observations.quote: we being destitute of wisdome know not that wood wherewith our life might be cherished and prolonged
observations.note: 'wood' is carried over from the fire comparison to stand for the unknown thing by which life is cherished and prolonged; we lack the wisdom to know it.

observations.quote: did attaine to so many ages, not by Nature and property of Time, for then all had been Long-liv'd, but by the help of Secrets and by Wisdome which was revealed but to few
observations.note: Adam and many of his time reached great ages not by Nature or the property of the time but by Secrets and Wisdome; they also lived a more frugall life than we.

observations.quote: by Wisdome which was revealed but to few, and by speciall knowledge which God gave them in this particular
observations.note: The wisdom that lengthened life was revealed to few only, as a special knowledge given by God.

observations.quote: Many holy men used this universall Medicine before the flood
observations.note: The Medicine is named universall and said to have been used by many holy men before the flood.

observations.name: Lactantius
observations.quote: which Adam also had in his Family, as Lactantius witnesseth
observations.note: Lactantius is named as witness that Adam had the Medicine in his family; the text does not show whether his witness also covers the holy men before the flood.

observations.quote: which strengthneth the Internall Balsom, and like Fire congregateth Homogeneous things, and segregateth Heterogeneous, which are of a contrary nature
observations.note: What the universall Medicine works: it strengthens the Internall Balsom and, like Fire, gathers like things and parts unlike ones.

observations.quote: Nor are we to relie upon their judgements, who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water
observations.note: Croll rejects the judgement of those ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water.

observations.name: they who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water
observations.quote: dream that the Deluge washed away the efficacy of fruits & of growing things, or that the power and strength of mens bodies was spoyled by the Water
observations.voice: QUOTED: they who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water
observations.note: A view of unnamed people, reported in order to reject it: that the Deluge took away the efficacy of growing things or the strength of men's bodies.

observations.quote: all things that grow by the benefit of Water do yet sprout and spring forth in the same vigour and with the same efficacy as they did in Adams time.
observations.note: Growing things have the same vigour and efficacy now as in Adam's time.

observations.quote: Wherefore we want nothing but the knowledge of Secrets, and their use
observations.note: All that is lacking is the knowledge of Secrets and of their use.

observations.quote: the Flood did not wast the things that grow, but wash'd away our wisdome of knowing them
observations.note: The Flood took away not the things that grow but the wisdom of knowing them.

observations.quote: These most secret of secrets have ever been hid from the common sort of them that professe Phylosophy, and especially sincemen began to abuse Wisdome, using it to an ill end
observations.note: The most secret of secrets have always been hidden from the common sort of those who profess Phylosophy, the more so since men began to abuse Wisdome.

observations.quote: wise men lived together in the Centre reserving wisdome among themselves, but banished those that had it not into the circumference
observations.note: When men multiplied, the wise kept wisdom among themselves in the Centre and banished those without it to the circumference.

observations.name: Paracels.
observations.quote: Paracels.
observations.note: The note on the wise in the Centre ends with the name Paracels.

observations.quote: as few reach the Naturall Terme, so also few have known the reason of prolonging the life
observations.note: Few reach the Naturall Terme and few have known the reason of prolonging life.

observations.quote: the life is broken off, or shortned, two manner of wayes
observations.note: Announces two ways life is broken off or shortened; CH6.73 and CH6.74 give them as First and Secondly.

observations.quote: MENS & ENS abrumpunt nobis vitam
observations.note: A Latin margin note at the head of the first way names MENS and ENS together; the paragraphs beside it name the two ways as the MIND (CH6.73) and PER ENTEM, the Being (CH6.74).

observations.quote: by the MIND, whence arise mentall diseases which are invisible, and affect us in our Mind
observations.note: Mental diseases are those arising from the mind: invisible, affecting us in the mind.

observations.quote: as Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence; Superstition, all which proceed from a spirituall affection
observations.note: Five mental diseases are listed, all from a spirituall affection.

observations.quote: No corporall guard or shelter availeth any thing against such like violences, but onely Faith which is able to resist them
observations.note: Nothing bodily guards against these; only Faith resists them.

observations.quote: some other Magicall means is requisite against witchcrafts and to cure those that are bewitched, and though the cure be difficult, yet is it possible
observations.note: Besides Faith, some Magicall means is needed against witchcrafts and for the bewitched; the cure is hard but possible.

observations.quote: that the act of the imagination is immanent, and that one mans body cannot be altered by another mans imagination
observations.note: The note reports an objection, of no named speaker ('what may be said'), and sets it aside with 'Notwithstanding': that imagination stays within and cannot alter another man's body. Kind corrected from position: the quoted words are the objection, not the note's own claim.

observations.quote: these diseases which only Adept Physitians know, are healed without the help of Natural Physick
observations.note: The mental diseases are known to Adept Physitians only, and healed without Natural Physick.

observations.quote: in the minds of men there is a kind of a hidden Virtue, of changing, attracting, and binding that which it desireth
observations.note: A hidden Virtue in men's minds changes, attracts and binds what it desires, most of all when set to work with the greatest excess of Imagination and Will.

observations.quote: the Antipathicall Loadstone, which doth (as it were) bewitch spiritually and invisibly
observations.note: 'bewitch' is marked by '(as it were)' as not meant plainly of the Loadstone; the loadstone is brought as a known case to make the mind's hidden Virtue no strange thing.

observations.quote: these five supernatural mischiefs
observations.note: The mental diseases are counted as five and called supernatural mischiefs that could suffocate our spirit.

observations.quote: i. e. Inchantment, Imagination, Estimation, Influence, Superstition
observations.note: The margin says which the five supernatural mischiefs are.

observations.quote: their malignant Astra's must be averted by a supernaturall cure and magicall help into something else, without any prophanation of Gods Name
observations.note: Against the five mischiefs their malignant Astra's are turned away into something else by a supernatural cure and magical help, without profaning God's Name; the lines given do not say how.

observations.quote: those diseases that proceed from the Mind require a mentall cure
observations.note: Diseases from the Mind need a mentall cure.

observations.name: Paracels.
observations.quote: of which see more in Paracels. his Philosophia Sagaci
observations.note: For more on the mentall cure the reader is sent to a writing of Paracels. named Philosophia Sagaci.

observations.quote: Godlinesse is the chiefest remedy, guard, and preservation against such like evills
observations.note: Godlinesse is the chief remedy against these evils, and God's help the best preservative in all diseases.

observations.quote: by the Being, as by Entall or Corporall diseases
observations.note: The second way, headed PER ENTEM, is by the Being, that is by Entall or Corporall diseases. Margin note N312 beside it is two gaps and cannot be read.

observations.quote: many who live to eate onely, and prefer a voluptuous superfluity before the Naturall necessity which is content and satisfied with a little, have surfeted themselves to death
observations.note: Many shorten life by excess in eating; natural necessity is content with little.

observations.quote: Health is preserved by fastings, and a moderate Diet is the best Governance to prolong the life
observations.note: Fasting keeps health and a moderate Diet is the best Governance for prolonging life.

observations.quote: is to be sought from Natural causes and means, to wit, from the Elements and hidden Secrets
observations.note: The cure of bodily harms from the Ens or Being is to be sought from natural causes and means, named as the Elements and hidden Secrets.

observations.quote: Corporall medicines doe no good to mentall or supernaturall distempers, nor can mentall medicines be profitable to bodily diseases
observations.note: Each kind of disease needs its own kind of cure.

observations.quote: all diseases require their own proper cure, and reject any other remedy
observations.note: Here every disease needs its own proper cure and rejects any other; CH6.71 speaks of one universall Medicine that may chase away all diseases which cause the naturall death. The lines given do not say how the two stand together.

observations.name: Theophrastus
observations.quote: by many various accidents may we be hindred and kept from attaining to the Naturall Term of life, as Theophrastus in his Books very often observeth
observations.note: Theophrastus is named as often observing in his Books that corruption in the womb, in birth and education, and many accidents keep us from the Naturall Term of life.

observations.quote: wander wider then the bounds of a Preface, I shall now draw to a conclusion
observations.note: The text calls itself a Preface with bounds and announces its conclusion.

observations.quote: divine Misteries are far greater than to be set forth by the splendor of mans words
observations.note: Divine Misteries are greater than man's words can set forth.

observations.quote: I have inserted in their proper places in this Prolix and Admonitory Preface
observations.note: Croll names the writing and says the gain of his labours, watchings, studies and peregrinations is set in its proper places within it. Kind for A65 corrected from cross-reference: it names the whole writing in hand, not another place.

observations.quote: so far as was lawfull, and so much as was allowable by God, have I imparted candidly from the intimate and inmost Armory or Treasury of my Heart
observations.note: He has imparted only as far as was lawful and allowed by God, and as far as divine Minerva hath given leave: a stated limit on what is told.

observations.quote: to the Children of Learning and Heirs of Wisdome, who with second thoughts which are the wisest
observations.note: The readers for whom it is imparted are named: the Children of Learning and Heirs of Wisdome, who go through these things with second thoughts and a pure mind.

observations.quote: reading them over in the light of God, without any superfluity or diminution, by often reiterated and evident speculations
observations.note: How the text asks to be read: in the light of God, adding and taking away nothing, with often repeated consideration.

observations.quote: Read them over and over, & over again, and againe; I hope it shall not repent thee of thy paines
observations.note: The margin tells the reader to read these things many times over.

observations.quote: it concerns the publick good to make known also in publick writing what belongs to the publick
observations.note: It is not enough to know for oneself; what belongs to the public should be made known in public writing, not from pride but for posterity's instruction and the honour of God's bounty.

observations.quote: We ought not to prefer our private profit before the publick good
observations.note: The margin states the rule of public good before private profit.

observations.quote: I see it taught in publick Schools for the most part rather for the glory of Education, than the good and profit of the Auditors
observations.note: One of his reasons for publishing: in the public Schools it is taught mostly for the glory of Education, not for the hearers' good.

observations.quote: The School of Physick is not covered with tile, but with the Firmament
observations.note: The margin says the School of Physick has the Firmament, not tile, for its roof.

observations.quote: I lived freely to the great advantage of my studies above ten years in two of the very best and most honourable Families
observations.note: More than ten years of free study in two families, which he ascribes to the assistance of the divine Majesty.

observations.quote: in that of ESNE at Lyons in France, and in that of BAPPENHEIMIE in the Segniory of Mareschall
observations.note: The two families are named; there he instructed the noble offspring entrusted to him and travelled, in particular with MAXIMILIAN, whose father Conradus was then a prisoner in Mareschal. Kind for A74 corrected from marking: a statement about himself.

observations.quote: that Physitian that walketh according to the mind of Paracelsus is onely able to open the Book of Nature
observations.note: Only the physician who follows the mind of Paracelsus can open the Book of Nature.

observations.quote: I had special and private converse with learned men, a thing most long'd for by a Physitian that desireth chiefly to turn over the BOOK of NATURE
observations.note: On his travels he had private converse with learned men, to whom he would hardly have been admitted but for the Relation he was then in.

observations.quote: the BOOK of NATURE (in which every region is a leaf) not profunctorily & superficially, but practically and experimentally
observations.note: The text says how its BOOK of NATURE is meant: every region is a leaf of it, and it is to be turned over practically and experimentally.

observations.quote: Heroick Prince CHRISTIAN ANHALTIN, with his more then singular favor and laudable patronage toward the more secret Studies, supplyed me with necessary expences
observations.note: Croll names his patron, who paid the necessary expenses out of favour toward the more secret Studies, and sets him down as a pattern for other great men.

observations.quote: all these Medicins come to, which must be prepar'd and try'd by Fire
observations.note: The medicines must be prepared and tried by Fire, at a cost he says he could not bear alone; nothing more of the work is given in these lines.

observations.quote: By which singular care toward the whole Spagyrick state
observations.note: The text names a Spagyrick state toward which the patron's care is shown; later the paragraph speaks of citizens of the Physicall & Spagyrick State and profession.

observations.quote: in respect of what concerns the order and Disposition of medicaments, I have proposed and set down this to my selfe
observations.note: He speaks of an order and disposition of medicaments he has set down after his own judgement; the lines given do not show where that ordered matter stands.

observations.quote: It will be safe for every man to add hereunto the further Experiences of his own, and dispose it otherwise according to his discretion for his private use
observations.note: Every man may add his own experiences and order the matter otherwise for his private use.

observations.quote: this harvest of Chymicall Corn, and the First fruits of my increase, and this Spagyrick present of my difficult and laborious diligence
observations.what: this harvest of Chymicall Corn, and the First fruits of my increase, and this Spagyrick present
observations.note: Three names Croll gives his work, which he thinks the best thing he could leave to his Country and Common-wealth.

observations.quote: will be most acceptable to godly learned men (for I regard not Hogs & Dogs that have no grace nor goodnes at all, those Beetles which I leave to their own dunghil)
observations.note: The work is meant for godly learned men; others, called Hogs, Dogs and Beetles, he does not regard.

observations.quote: who have been train'd up in the Spagyrick and Hermetick School of Vulcan, being not yet deprived of the Light of understanding
observations.note: The readers it suits most: those trained in the Spagyrick and Hermetick School of Vulcan and taught by approved Authors in the general rules of Physitians; 'before observed' may point back to an earlier place, the lines given do not show it.

observations.quote: I have not handled all things here in this place, to avoyd prolixity; I know there are not a few doubts left unresolved
observations.note: He has not handled everything here and doubts are left unresolved; the reason he gives is to avoid length.

observations.quote: It is provided for by the Philosophical law that some tedious things should be left obscure to young Schollers and for intelligent & wise men to find out
observations.note: By a Philosophical law some things are left obscure on purpose, for the wise to find out; their wits are thereby tried and made fit for the School of Phylosophers.

observations.quote: He that can receive it let him receive it; and he that doth not understand, let him either learn or hold his peace and be silent
observations.note: The text is for the one who can receive it; whoever does not understand is to learn or be silent.

observations.quote: the young Pupil that is a diligent Searcher out of the Ancient First & Sacred Phylosophy
observations.note: The philosophy the pupil searches out is named Ancient, First and Sacred; the pupil is to fear God, lay aside his Phantasie and have his Reason well disposed.

observations.quote: he may apprehend & conjecture the signification of MANY things by a Few in this open market of Nature, not by a vulgar sharpsightednes but by the assistance of the Almighty
observations.note: A few things signify many, which the fit pupil may conjecture with God's help and not by common sharpness: the reader is told to infer many things from few.

observations.quote: the doors and Inner rooms are unlockt to him by the favorable virtue of the most high Creator
observations.note: To the one who reads sincerely and examines inwardly, doors and Inner rooms are unlocked by the Creator: there is an inside that opens to some readers only.

observations.quote: from all these things rightly understood, through PRAYER & PAINS, shall reap much more fruit than he expected
observations.note: Rightly understood, through PRAYER and PAINS, these things yield more fruit than the reader expected.

observations.quote: I have not spoken of so many things, but there yet more left to be spaken
observations.note: More is left to be spoken than has been spoken.

observations.quote: These things are writen for them who by aprospicocious & happy wit have their mind inlightned by God
observations.note: These things are written for those whose mind God has enlightened and whose soul is seasoned with the salt of Wisdome.

observations.quote: A few things or words are sufficient for him that understandeth
observations.note: Few words suffice the one who understands: the reader is to take more than is said.

observations.name: any of a contrary opinion
observations.quote: reproaching them for a patch'd and mixt hodg podg of good & bad together
observations.voice: QUOTED: any of a contrary opinion
observations.note: A reproach Croll foresees from those of a contrary opinion and rejects: that such labours are a patched mixture of good and bad. He likens their censures to Aesop's Crow and their temper to Timon that Man-hater.

observations.quote: to get the corn from the chaffe, and separate true from false, is sometime a most tedious and difficult task
observations.note: Against critics who call the work a mixture of good and bad, he says sorting true from false is at times tedious and difficult.

observations.quote: who (as already before) are justly to be casheer'd
observations.note: 'as already before' points back to an earlier place where such opponents were dismissed; the lines given do not show it.

observations.quote: let them take their lited candle from under the bushel, lest the curse of the figtree befall them
observations.note: Those who would discourage others are told to open their own fountains and publish their own observations.

observations.name: Mat.
observations.note: The margin names a place in a writing, Mat. 21.19, beside the curse of the figtree.

observations.quote: whose purpose is not to find out that which is True but to wrangle about it
observations.note: He sets aside contentions of words, Scholastick questions and fruitless disputations as the way of the Sceptick Phylosopher, who seeks wrangling and not what is true.

observations.quote: to bring forth better things than these out of their own experience
observations.note: Others are to be spurred by his example, as good citizens of the Physicall & Spagyrick State and profession, to bring out better things from their own experience.

observations.quote: for surely Physick is not yet come to the Limit of perfection, but many things remain to be discovered to future ages
observations.note: Physick is not yet perfect; much remains for future ages to discover.

observations.quote: For who can find out the end of Physick
observations.note: No one can find the end of Physick.

observations.quote: to succor poor Lazarus, not wth Sylogistical or Levitical Words, but with a Samaritan Help & Ayd
observations.note: The sick are to be helped with deeds, not words, said through the figures of Lazarus, Levitical words and Samaritan help. Kind for A99 corrected from local signal: the text does not mark the figure.

observations.quote: cast away the Signatures of cursed Sloth, of Drones, in their hollow cracks and clamors which at least make a terrible noyse, they may become Bees
observations.note: Drones and Bees are used in a second sense for the idle, noisy opponents and for those who work; the text marks sloth and noise as the Signatures of Drones.

observations.quote: conspire together with us into an union and Spagyrick mellifice divorcing the multitude and abstaining from all fornication
observations.note: Following the Bees figure, the joint work is called a Spagyrick mellifice. 'divorcing the multitude' and 'fornication' stand in a passage about agreement in work, not about bodies. Interpreted (the readers' inference, the narrowest): the words are figurative for a union kept apart from the crowd and from what is foreign to it; the text does not itself say what they mean.

observations.quote: Really & indeed may maintain & defend the Excellency of Chymistry against all that reproach it
observations.note: Those who join are to defend the Excellency of Chymistry against its reproachers and to better his endeavour without envy.

observations.quote: after other secret Sciences which yet lie in the dark
observations.note: Other secret Sciences are said still to lie in the dark.

observations.quote: that Ancient, True, & Philosophical Medicin, which by reason of the long continuance and injury of time, as also the unworthines of our age (mens sins doubtles so meeting together) is not yet fully known
observations.note: The Medicine is named once more at the close, Ancient, True and Philosophical, and said to be not yet fully known through the injury of time and the unworthiness of the age.

observations.quote: may in a shorttime by the heavenly assistance, be restored to its lost lustre & ancient splendor
observations.note: He expects the Medicine may soon, by heavenly help, be restored to its ancient splendour, for the good of mankind and the honour of Spagyrick Phisitians.

observations.quote: whose endeavor & pains that immense sea of divine Mercy would be pleased to make use of as an Instrument & Pen to accomplish so healthful and saving a work
observations.note: The Spagyrick physicians' pains are wished to be God's Instrument and Pen for this work.

observations.quote: it concerns the publick good to make known also in publick writing what belongs to the publick
observations.note: Here what belongs to the public is to be made known in public writing; the same paragraph says some things are left obscure by the Philosophical law and that he imparted only so far as was lawful, and CH6.71 says the most secret of secrets have ever been hid from the common sort. The lines given do not show where the line between the two is drawn.

observations.quote: Which that holy Triunity grant, whose unspeakable Name be blessed for ever and ever
observations.note: Closing prayer that the holy Triunity grant what the last paragraph hopes for.

observations.quote: AMEN
observations.note: The last word of the text given; the Preface ends.

dropped.reason: A figure only; the text marks no signal of how to read it, so the kind is not borne out.
Not a conflict: the paragraph itself sets the two apart as the Naturall death and the Fatall death, as B15's own note says.

voices.basis: Porta named as rejecting an opinion and 'affirming' the contrary.

voices.quote: It is the conservation of the Human body
voices.basis: The note opens by naming the writing Archid. of the Elixirs; it does not show whether the lines after it are drawn from it.
Verb of saying with the name.

voices.quote: as we may preserve a little fire by laying on more wood
voices.basis: Follows 'Paracelsus saith' after a colon, through 'know not that wood wherewith our life might be cherished and prolonged'; the text does not show where his words end.

voices.quote: which Adam also had in his Family

voices.voice: QUOTED: they who being ignorant of the Mysteries of the Element of Water
voices.quote: dream that the Deluge washed away the efficacy of fruits
voices.basis: A view reported to be rejected: 'Nor are we to relie upon their judgements'.

voices.quote: When men multiplyed in the world
voices.basis: The note ends with the name Paracels.

voices.quote: that the act of the imagination is immanent
voices.basis: An objection brought as 'what may be said' and set aside by 'Notwithstanding'; no speaker named.

voices.quote: that many times weare corrupted in our mothers womb
voices.basis: 'as Theophrastus in his Books very often observeth'.

voices.voice: QUOTED: any of a contrary opinion
voices.quote: reproaching them for a patch'd and mixt hodg podg of good & bad together
voices.basis: A reproach Croll foresees from 'any of a contrary opinion' and rejects.

voices.quote: lest the curse of the figtree befall them
voices.basis: Margin note N318 names Mat. 21.19 at these words.
